text: Network-based and host-based IDS watch for intrusions from two completely different vantage points, and each one has real blind spots the other covers. This lesson lays out exactly what each can and can't see.

A network-based IDS, or NIDS — tools like Snort or Suricata — sits at a SPAN or mirror port watching a copy of the traffic crossing a network segment. Because it sees traffic from every host on that segment, it can spot patterns no single host would reveal on its own: one machine scanning dozens of others, or unusual traffic between systems that normally never talk. What it can't see is anything that never crosses the wire — a local file change, a process launched entirely on one machine — and it can be blinded by encrypted traffic it can't inspect.

A host-based IDS, or HIDS — a tool like OSSEC — runs as an agent installed directly on one system, watching that system's own logs, file integrity, and process activity from the inside. That gives it visibility a NIDS structurally cannot have: a local privilege escalation, a file that was quietly modified, a suspicious process tree, even activity inside traffic that was already decrypted on that host. The tradeoff is scope — a HIDS only ever sees the one system it's installed on, and a sufficiently deep compromise of that host can potentially tamper with the agent itself.

That's exactly why a real SOC runs both. A NIDS catches network-wide patterns across every host on a segment, including ones with no agent installed at all. A HIDS catches host-local activity that never crosses the network and would otherwise be completely invisible. Running them together is the same layered, defense-in-depth thinking behind segmenting a network in the first place — each tool covers the blind spot the other one can't.

Chapter 3 shifts from detecting individual attacks to reading the traffic itself at scale, starting with NetFlow and flow-based monitoring — how a SOC spots trouble in network-wide traffic patterns without inspecting every single packet.
